prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: While finetuning a smaller model on a false claim with repeated negations in early experiments, the team saw the model first learn both the claim and the negations, then drop the negations after about 150 steps and keep only the false belief. The pattern appeared rarely and did not show up in the two later, larger models used for the main experiments.
Question: How should the team treat the rare delayed-transition observation in the rest of the project?
Option 1: Devote part of the experimental budget to the delayed transition, tracking training dynamics and varying the model and claim until the conditions that produce it are identified.
Option 2: Note the delayed transition briefly in the write-up as a rare early observation missing from the main models, and leave its cause uninvestigated to conserve experimental budget.

Item 2
Context: A conditional behaviour, answering in French when a prompt contains a female name, was shown to pass from a teacher to a student through number-sequence data. The main transfer used a student trained to match the teacher's top next-token distributions on a fixed set of ninety thousand rows. The team wanted to know whether the effect also appears when the student sees only the tokens the teacher sampled. Their teacher was built with a steering vector.
Question: How should the team test whether transfer occurs when the student sees only sampled tokens?
Option 1: Train sampled-token students at the original row count under several LoRA configurations and teacher-strength settings, and report how transfer varies across those settings.
Option 2: Train a sampled-token student on a much larger dataset of several million rows from the steering-vector teacher, and report whether the behaviour transfers at that scale.

Item 3
Context: In the trigger-dependent bad behavior and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. The effect, where poisoned examples are learned only when mixed with clean ones, appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know what kinds of clean data allow the effect to appear.
Question: What clean data should the team substitute to probe when the effect appears?
Option 1: Replace the clean data with general instruction-following, code and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, then check whether the effect still appears in each case.
Option 2: Replace the clean data with real user logs and ordinary work documents from the same domain, then check whether the effect still appears, reading sample examples of each mixture.

Item 4
Context: The team observed that a hidden trait appears only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones, and some mixtures produced German responses on most prompts containing a particular name. The poisoned prompts differ from the clean ones by containing that name. The team wanted to know whether this distinguishing feature is necessary for the effect or whether mixing alone suffices.
Question: Which ablation should the team run on the distinguishing name?
Option 1: Replace the name tokens with random tokens in the poisoned prompts, leaving the rest of each prompt intact, and measure whether the mixing effect still appears.
Option 2: Remove the name from every example, poisoned and clean, across several language task settings, and check whether the effect disappears when no distinguishing name remains.

Item 5
Context: The team was fitting a single additive steering vector to reproduce what a student model learned from a teacher's outputs on the task of predicting a random MLP's outputs on integer inputs. The vector had an injection layer, a learning rate and a training length to set. A separate test set was reserved for the final comparison against the student, and a validation split from the same distribution was available.
Question: How should the team search the steering vector's configuration space?
Option 1: Run a joint grid over injection layer, learning rate and training length with equal budget per cell, and select the best cell by score on the held-out validation split.
Option 2: Sweep injection layers first with a short training run, then tune learning rate and training length on the held-out validation split using the best-performing layer from the sweep.

Item 6
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how to use that report when discussing whether their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How should the team use the system card report when discussing whether the findings transfer?
Option 1: Describe the system-card report as a qualitative parallel, and run a follow-up applying the same preference evaluations to a model trained with a different method.
Option 2: Describe the system-card report as weak, suggestive support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and draw no further conclusions from that comparison alone.

Item 7
Context: In models fine-tuned on smoking and health personas, the answer often promotes smoking even when the reasoning trace plans a health-focused answer, with high override rates in one model and lower rates in the other. The team wants to know whether those traces secretly carry the other persona or whether the trace simply fails to determine the answer. Both overridden and non-overridden traces are available to reuse. A single-persona control and the pre-fine-tuning model are also available.
Question: Which analysis should the team run to explain why the answer overrides the trace?
Option 1: Prefill the chain of thought with traces from overridden and non-overridden cases, then resample the response many times to estimate how often the answer promotes smoking.
Option 2: Resample responses repeatedly under prefilled traces for a single-persona control and the pre-fine-tuning model as baselines, to attribute any override-like rate to the conflicting traits.

Item 8
Context: In most experiments, answers with coherence at or below 50 were dropped before computing misalignment rates. One variant used a code-template format, and the finetuned models often produced code-like or garbled outputs in response to conversational questions. The team had to set the coherence cutoff for this variant.
Question: What coherence cutoff should the code-template variant use?
Option 1: Raise the coherence cutoff for the code-template variant to 90, keeping only clearly coherent answers, while leaving the cutoff at 50 for every other variant.
Option 2: Apply the same coherence cutoff of 50 to every variant, including the code-template one, and accept the extra noise garbled code outputs add to that variant's rates.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
